cards.meaning: An object representing the eventual success value or failure reason of an async operation. It lets you attach handlers that run later as microtasks instead of nesting callbacks — one object for not-done-yet / ok / failed, plus standard combinators and async/await.

pending → fulfilled with value or rejected with reason. Exactly one transition out of pending. After that, further resolve/reject calls are ignored; the outcome is immutable. Later handlers still run with the settled result, scheduled as microtasks.

cards.front: When does the Promise executor run?
cards.meaning: Synchronously when the Promise is constructed. resolve/reject are typically called later from host callbacks. throw inside the executor rejects the Promise — same as calling reject.
cards.example: new Promise(() => { throw new Error('boom'); }).catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // 'boom'

cards.meaning: resolve(x) fulfills with x, or adopts/flattens if x is a Promise. reject(r) rejects with reason r. Promise.resolve(1) is already fulfilled; Promise.resolve(otherPromise) adopts it; Promise.reject(err) is already rejected. Use them to wrap values or normalize maybe-Promise APIs.

Returns a new Promise — it does not mutate the original. If the source fulfills, onFulfilled runs as a microtask. If the source rejects and onRejected is provided, that runs instead. Missing handlers pass the outcome through to the returned Promise.
.catch(onRejected) is equivalent to .then(undefined, onRejected). Prefer .catch for readability when you only handle errors.

Runs on either fulfillment or rejection — cleanup (hide spinners, release locks), not primary result logic. Downstream still fulfills with the original value if onFinally succeeds and doesn't return a rejecting Promise. Downstream rejects with the original reason if the source rejected, unless onFinally throws/rejects, which can override.

cards.front: What you return from onFulfilled becomes?
cards.meaning: The fulfillment value of the Promise returned by that .then — unless you return a Promise, which is flattened/adopted. Next .then receives the inner fulfillment value, not a nested Promise. You do not get Promise<Promise<T>> in the handler chain.

Returned Promise rejects with that error (same as returning Promise.reject(err)). Rejection skips onFulfilled-only .then handlers until a .catch or .then(..., onRejected) — like try/catch across the chain. A handling .catch that returns a value recovers: the next link fulfills, the error stops propagating.

Promise reactions (.then/.catch/.finally) run as microtasks after the current call stack clears, before the next macrotask. Even Promise.resolve(1) does not run handlers inline — they still queue. Common trap: assuming .then runs synchronously on an already-fulfilled Promise.
cards.example: Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('micro')); setTimeout(() => console.log('macro'), 0); console.log('sync'); // sync, micro, macro

cards.meaning: all: fail fast (any rejection); result is values in input order; empty array fulfills with []. allSettled: collect all outcomes (never rejects from a child). race: first settle (fulfill or reject) — timeouts. any: first success (AggregateError if all fail). Match failure policy to the product requirement. Combinators overlap host waiting, not parallel JS on one stack.

cards.front: Promise.all vs allSettled for partial UI?
cards.meaning: all rejects when any one rejects — you lose successful branches. Other in-flight work may still continue; all does not cancel siblings unless you abort separately. allSettled always fulfills once all settle with {status, value} | {status, reason}. Profile + settings in parallel, render whatever arrived: allSettled, not all.

cards.front: race vs any when first result is rejection?
cards.meaning: race settles with the first fulfillment or rejection — a fast failure beats a slow success. Timeout pattern: Promise.race([promise, timeoutReject]). any keeps waiting for a fulfillment unless all fail (then AggregateError). Using race when you meant any is the common mistake.

A settled rejected Promise with no rejection handler yet — runtime warnings / hard fails depending on environment. Always end chains that can reject: doWork().catch(handle), not a bare doWork() if it can reject.

cards.front: Does a mid-chain .catch swallow and continue?
cards.meaning: Yes unless it rethrows. load().then(transform).catch(showError).then(maybeContinue) — the catch handles load OR transform failures, then maybeContinue runs after catch unless catch rethrows. Know whether that swallow is intended.

cards.front: Nesting getX().then inside .then vs returning getX()?
cards.meaning: then(() => { getX().then(...) }) breaks flattening and error propagation. Return the Promise: then(() => getX()) so the chain flattens and errors propagate.
